html:
A water-driven astronomical clock tower built at Kaifeng, the capital of Song China, by the official and scholar Su Song from 1088. It was one of the most complex machines of the medieval world.

The tower stood several storeys high. A large water wheel turned it, and an escapement held the wheel and released it one step at a time, so it moved at a steady pace. The drive turned a bronze armillary sphere on the roof for watching the stars, a celestial globe inside, and a stack of wooden figures that rang bells, beat drums and showed signs to mark the hours. A chain drive carried power up the tower.

The escapement idea went back to the Tang monk Yi Xing in the 700s, but Su Song joined it into a full clock. He wrote a book with detailed drawings of it, which survives.

When the Jurchens took Kaifeng in 1127 they carried the clock north, and no one could make it run again. Mechanical clocks with escapements appeared in Europe about two centuries later.
sum: A water-driven astronomical clock tower built at Kaifeng, the capital of Song China, by the official and scholar Su Song from 1088. It was one of the most complex machines of the medieval world.
